source_text: Sed nec inter consuetudines dispicere voluerunt illi sanctissimi antecessores. Tamen tolerabilius apud nos ad usque proxime utrique consuetudini communicabatur. Arbitrio permissa res erat, ut quaeque voluisset aut tegi aut prostitui, sicut et nubere, quod et ipsum neque cogitur neque prohibetur. Contenta erat veritas pacisci cum consuetudine, ut tacite sub consuetudinis nomine frueretur se vel ex parte. Sed quoniam coeperat agnitio proficere, ut per licentiam utriusque moris indicium melioris partis emergeret, statim ille adversarius bonorum multoque institutorum opus suum fecit. Ambiunt virgines hominum adversus virgines dei nuda plane fronte temerariam in audaciam excitatae, et virgines videntur quae aliquid a viris petere possunt, nedum tale factum, ut scilicet aemulae earum, tanto magis liberae quanto Christi solius ancillae, dedantur illis. Scandalizamur, inquiunt, quia aliter aliae incedunt, et malunt scandalizari quam provocari, Scandalum, nisi fallor, non bonae rei, sed malae exemplum est, aedificans ad delictum. Bonae res neminem scandalizant, nisi malam mentem. Si bonum est modestia, verecundia, fastidium gloriae, soli deo captans placere, agnoscant malum suum quae de tali bono scandalizantur Quid enim, si et incontinentes dicant se a continentibus scandalizari, continentia revocanda est? Et ne multinubi scandalizentur, monogamia recusanda est? Cur non magis hae quaerantur scandalo sibi esse petulantiam, impudentiam ostentaticiae virginitatis? Propter eiusmodi igitur capita nundinaticia trahantur virgines sanctae in ecclesiam, erubescentes quod cognoscantur in medio, paventes quod detegantur accersitae quasi ad stuprum. Non minus enim et hoc pati nolunt. Omnis publicatio virginis bonae stupri passio est, et tamen vim carnis pati minus est, quia de officio naturae venit. Sed cum spiritus ipse violatur in virgine sublato velamine, didicit amittere quod tuebatur. O sacrilegae manus, quae dicatum deo habitum detrahere potuerunt! Quid peius aliquis persecutor fecisset, si hoc a virgine electum cognovisset? Denudasti puellam a capite, et tota iam virgo sibi non est, alia est facta. Exsurge igitur veritas, exsurge et quasi de patientia erumpe! Nullam volo consuetudinem defendas; nam iam et illa, sub qua te fruebaris, expugnatur. Te esse demonstra quae virgines tegit. Ipsa scripturas tuas interpretare, quas consuetudo non novit. Si enim nosset, nunquam esset.
thought_title: Truth must break out against custom
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the church's past tolerance of both veiled and unveiled virgins, and now turns to rebuke those who are scandalized by the better practice.
pass_a_gloss: But not even among customs did those most holy predecessors wish to look into the matter. Nevertheless it was more tolerable among us up to very recently that both customs were shared in. The matter had been left to choice, so that each woman might wish either to be veiled or to be displayed, just as also to marry, which itself is neither forced nor forbidden. Truth was content to make a pact with custom, so that silently under the name of custom it might enjoy itself even in part. But since knowledge had begun to advance, so that through the license of both ways the indication of the better part might emerge, immediately that adversary of good things and of many established practices did his work. Virgins of men strive against virgins of God, with plainly bare forehead, stirred up into rash boldness, and they seem to be virgins who can ask something from men, much less such a deed, so that of course their rivals, so much more free as servants of Christ alone, may be handed over to them. We are scandalized, they say, because some walk differently from others, and they prefer to be scandalized than to be provoked. Scandal, unless I am mistaken, is not an example of a good thing, but of a bad thing, building toward sin. Good things scandalize no one, except a bad mind. If modesty is good, and shamefastness, and disdain of glory, seeking to please God alone, let those recognize their own evil who are scandalized by such a good. For what, if also the incontinent should say that they are scandalized by the continent, is continence to be called back? And so that the often-married may not be scandalized, is monogamy to be refused? Why should not rather these things be sought as a scandal to themselves: wantonness, shamelessness of virginity put on display? On account of such heads therefore, marketable heads, let holy virgins be dragged into the church, blushing because they are recognized in the midst, trembling because they are uncovered, summoned as if to defilement. For no less do they not wish to suffer this too. Every public display of a good virgin is a suffering of defilement, and yet to suffer violence of the flesh is less, because it comes from the office of nature. But when the spirit itself is violated in a virgin by the removal of the veil, it has learned to lose what it was protecting. O sacrilegious hands, which have been able to strip off the attire dedicated to God! What worse would any persecutor have done, if he had known this was chosen by a virgin? You have stripped the girl from the head, and now the whole virgin is not herself, she has become another. Rise up therefore, truth, rise up and burst forth as if from patience! I do not want you to defend any custom; for now even that one, under which you were being enjoyed, is being attacked. Show that it is you who veils virgins. Yourself interpret your Scriptures, which custom does not know. For if it had known, it would never have existed.

choices.why: Tertullian uses the verb in its root sense of being put forth publicly, but the word carries the connotation of prostitution; 'displayed' keeps the public exposure while avoiding an over-literal 'prostituted' that would narrow the sense.
The adjective derives from market-day (nundinae) and suggests virgins being put on sale or display for public consumption; 'marketable' preserves the commercial metaphor.
The rare adjective ostentaticius means 'given to display'; rendering as 'display-virginity' keeps the compound force and the pejorative tone without smoothing it into a paraphrase.
Stuprum is sexual violation or defilement; passio is suffering. The phrase is deliberately strong and paradoxical; 'suffering of defilement' keeps both the violence and the sexual shame.

choices.english: burst forth as if from patience
choices.why: The image is of truth breaking out from the restraint it has long endured; 'burst forth as if from patience' preserves the quasi-personification and the force of erumpe.

pass_b_english: But those most holy predecessors of ours did not even want to examine the customs. Still, among us until very recently both customs were shared in with some tolerance. The matter was left to each person's choice, so that any woman could either be veiled or be displayed, just as she could marry—which itself is neither forced nor forbidden. Truth was content to make a pact with custom, so that under custom's name it could quietly enjoy itself, at least in part. But once knowledge began to advance, so that through the freedom of both practices the evidence of the better part might emerge, immediately that enemy of good things and of so many good institutions did his work. Virgins devoted to men compete against virgins of God, stirred up to reckless boldness with completely bare foreheads, and they are considered virgins who can ask something from men—let alone such a deed as this, that God's virgins, who are all the more free because they are servants of Christ alone, should be handed over to their rivals. "We are scandalized," they say, "because others walk about differently," and they prefer to be scandalized than to be provoked. Scandal, unless I am mistaken, is not the example of a good thing but of an evil thing, building toward sin. Good things scandalize no one except a bad mind. If modesty is good, and shamefastness, and contempt for glory, seeking to please God alone, then let those who are scandalized by such a good recognize their own evil. What if the incontinent were to say they are scandalized by the continent—should continence be called back? And so that the repeatedly married are not scandalized, must monogamy be rejected? Why do these women not rather complain that wantonness and the shamelessness of virginity put on display are a scandal to them? It is because of such heads put on display, then, that holy virgins are dragged into the church, blushing because they are recognized in the midst, trembling because they are uncovered when summoned, as if to defilement. For this too they do not want to suffer. Every public display of a good virgin is a form of defilement, and yet suffering violence to the flesh is less, because it comes from the working of nature. But when the spirit itself is violated in a virgin by the removal of her veil, she has learned to lose what she was protecting. O sacrilegious hands, which have been able to strip off a garment dedicated to God! What worse could any persecutor have done, if he had known this was chosen by a virgin? You have uncovered a girl from her head, and now the whole virgin is no longer herself; she has become another. Rise up, then, truth—rise up and burst forth as if from patience! I do not want you to defend any custom; for even that custom under which you were enjoying yourself is now being attacked. Show that you are the one who veils virgins. Interpret your own Scriptures yourself, which custom does not know. For if it had known them, it would never have existed.

problems.quote: Why should these women not rather complain that wantonness and the shamelessness of display-virginity are a scandal to themselves?
problems.source_quote: Cur non magis hae quaerantur scandalo sibi esse petulantiam, impudentiam ostentaticiae virginitatis?
problems.why: The Latin asks why these women should be considered a scandal for their own arrogance; the English adds that they should complain, changing the meaning.
problems.fix: Why should these women not be considered a scandal for their own arrogance and shameless display of virginity?

problems.why: Source asks 'must monogamy be rejected?' (deontic necessity), not a passive 'should it be refused'—the rhetorical force is obligation, not mere preference.
problems.ruling: Latin 'monogamia recusanda est?' uses gerundive 'recusanda est' = must be rejected, not merely 'should'

edits.old: Why should these women not rather complain that wantonness and the shamelessness of display-virginity are a scandal to themselves?
edits.new: Why should these women not rather be considered a scandal to themselves for their wantonness and the shamelessness of display-virginity?

fixed: Changed 'complain that... are a scandal to themselves' to 'be considered a scandal to themselves for...' to match the Latin 'quaerantur scandalo sibi esse petulantiam, impudentiam' (be sought as a scandal to themselves: wantonness, shamelessness).
Changed 'should monogamy be refused?' to 'must monogamy be rejected?' to match the deontic force of 'recusanda est' (must be rejected).

problems.why: The source lists modestia, verecundia, and contempt for glory; "reverence" is not present and adds a concept not in the Latin.
problems.fix: If modesty, verecundia, and contempt for glory, seeking to please God alone, then let those scandalized by such a good recognize their own evil.

problems.quote: should be handed over to those men
problems.why: Source says 'be handed over to them' (the virgins of men), not specifically 'those men'.
problems.fix: should be handed over to them
problems.ruling: ‘dedantur illis’ means ‘be handed over to them (the virgins)’, not ‘to those men’; referent changed.

edits.old: If modesty is good, and reverence, and contempt for glory, seeking to please God alone, then let those who are scandalized by such a good recognize their own evil.
edits.new: If modesty is good, and shamefastness, and contempt for glory, seeking to please God alone, then let those who are scandalized by such a good recognize their own evil.

edits.old: should be handed over to those men.
edits.new: should be handed over to them.

fixed: The source lists modestia, verecundia, fastidium gloriae; 'reverence' is not in the Latin, so replaced with 'shamefastness' for verecundia.
The source 'dedantur illis' means 'be handed over to them' (the virgins of men), not 'those men', so removed the added specificity.

problems.quote: "We are scandalized," they say, "because others walk about differently,"
problems.why: Unclear who 'they' are; could be opponents or unveiled virgins themselves.
problems.fix: Specify: opponents of veiling say this, or unveiled virgins' defenders say this.

problems.quote: Virgins of men compete against virgins of God
problems.why: 'Virgins of men' is not intelligible English; likely means pagan or secular virgins.
problems.fix: Render as 'Virgins devoted to men' or 'worldly virgins.'

problems.quote: and they are considered virgins who can ask something from men
problems.why: Sentence structure is confused; meaning is unclear.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'they are counted as virgins though they can make demands of men.'

problems.quote: let alone such a deed as this, that the rivals of God's virgins, who are all the more free because they are servants of Christ alone, should be handed over to them
problems.why: Syntax is tangled; unclear who is handed over to whom and why.
problems.fix: Rephrase for clarity: 'let alone that God's virgins should be handed over to their rivals.'

problems.quote: because the forehead of sin is harder, taught shamelessness by sin itself and in sin itself
problems.why: Metaphor is compressed to the point of unintelligibility.
problems.fix: Expand: 'because sin hardens the forehead, teaching shamelessness by its own practice.'

problems.quote: For no one would have approved that custom which denies virgins while it displays them, except people just like the virgins themselves
problems.why: 'Denies virgins while it displays them' is contradictory and unclear.
problems.fix: Clarify: 'which refuses to veil virgins while putting them on display.'

problems.quote: It is as much the mark of a holy man to blush if he has seen a virgin as it is of a holy virgin if she has been seen by a man.
problems.why: The comparison is grammatically tangled and hard to parse.
problems.fix: Rephrase: 'A holy man blushes at seeing a virgin just as a holy virgin blushes at being seen.'

problems.quote: Every public display of a good virgin is a suffering of defilement
problems.why: 'Suffering of defilement' is awkward; likely means 'a kind of defilement' or 'equivalent to being defiled.'
problems.fix: Render as 'is a form of defilement' or 'amounts to defilement.'

problems.quote: because it comes from the office of nature
problems.why: 'Office of nature' is odd; likely means 'function' or 'work' of nature.
problems.fix: Render as 'because it comes from the working of nature.'

problems.why: 'Marketable' sounds modern/commercial; likely means 'exposed for public viewing' or 'on display.'
problems.fix: Render as 'heads put on display' or 'heads offered for public viewing.'

problems.why: Hyphenated compound is not natural English; meaning is unclear.
problems.fix: Render as 'virginity put on display' or 'virginity that is shown off.'

problems.why: Multiple odd renderings for unveiled virgins or their practice; reader cannot connect them.
problems.fix: Use one consistent term like 'unveiled virgins' throughout.

problems.why: Deponent fruor: truth was enjoying itself under that custom, as earlier with se, not being enjoyed.
problems.fix: for even that custom under which you were enjoying yourself is now being attacked.
problems.ruling: Fruor is deponent: 'te fruebaris' means 'you were enjoying yourself'. The English passive 'you were being enjoyed' reverses the agency and contradicts the earlier 'frueretur se' rendering.

edits.old: for even that custom under which you were being enjoyed is now being attacked.
edits.new: for even that custom under which you were enjoying yourself is now being attacked.

fixed: agency: fixed to 'you were enjoying yourself' — 'sub qua te fruebaris' is deponent fruor with active sense, as with earlier 'frueretur se', not passive.

problems.quote: Why should these women not rather be considered a scandal to themselves
problems.source_quote: Cur non magis hae quaerantur scandalo sibi esse petulantiam
problems.why: 'quaerantur' means 'complain'. The women are told to complain that wantonness is a scandal to them. The English makes the women themselves the scandal.
problems.fix: Why do these women not rather complain that the wantonness and shamelessness of showy virginity is a scandal to them?
problems.ruling: hae querantur/quaerantur + esse petulantiam: they should complain that wantonness is the scandal; English makes the women the scandal.

edits.old: Why should these women not rather be considered a scandal to themselves for their wantonness and the shamelessness of virginity put on display?

fixed: Fixed mistranslation of 'Cur non magis hae quaerantur scandalo sibi esse petulantiam, impudentiam': wantonness/shamelessness is the scandal to them, not the women themselves.

last_rejected.ruling: stuprum = sexual violation; ‘defilement’ is a broader but acceptable rendering.

last_rejected.ruling: stupri passio = suffering of sexual violation; ‘defilement’ is a vague but not misleading gloss.

last_rejected.ruling: 'quaerantur' here is a spelling of queror (to complain). 'hae quaerantur … sibi esse petulantiam' is acc+inf after a verb of complaint, so 'complain that … a scandal to them' is correct.
